Clive Rice in India

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We follow Clive Rice to India for his final scan

Summary:
We follow Clive Rice as he travels to India for a final scan after having undergone Cyberknife therapy some months ago. Rice, a famous South African cricketer collapsed on the golf course and was told he had a brain tumour which was too deep to operate. Left with little options, he opted to go to India for Cyberknife therapy, a noninvasive robotic procedure that emits concentrated radiation to the tumor. Miraculously the treatment worked and Clive is on the road to recovery. He is also now raising funds to bring this revolutionary machine to South Africa so that others may benefit from it without having to travel overseas.

We will speak to doctors in India who treated him as well as patients in South Africa who have received Cyberknife therapy.

Press Release:


Clive Rice In India
He was one of the best all-round cricketers of his time. But today Clive Rice is a fragile man who has battled a cancer that had spread deep into his brain. Doctors had little hope for a recovery. But for Clive, defeat was not an option. In a race against time, he travelled to India for pioneering robotic Cyberknife laser treatment which concentrates radiation directly into the tumour. Was it successful? Carte Blanche joins Clive Rice as he returns to India for the final verdict.


Script:


CYBERKNIFE SCRIPT

9th of June. A fragile Clive Rice and his wife Sue board a flight. Destination: India. It’s all a far cry from the days when he was considered to be the best cricketing all-rounder in the world. Clive was a brilliant captain and tactician. But had his most recent strategy worked? He’d travelled to Bangalore three months earlier for cancer treatment and was now returning for a check-up. But, a week before the flight he had began to lose some movement on the left hand side of his body. He feared the worst. His battle with cancer began last year!.


CLIVE RICE – I was playing golf and suddenly I thought I had a pulled muscle in the side of my leg here.

It turned out to be a rare form of soft tissue cancer - a sarcoma. He underwent surgery on his leg but it had also spread to his lungs. Further painful surgery followed.

CLIVE RICE – If Heyneke Meyer is looking for someone who wants to play against the All Blacks, I’ll play because it can’t be that sore.

After grueling chemotherapy, it was then discovered that the cancer had spread to deep within his brain. Conventional radiation was not an option. His tumour was imoprrable. .

CLIVE RICE – When I fell over, I think the doctor said to Susan, you better call the Hospice in.

LINK – WHEN CLIVE RICE WAS CONFRONTED WITH THE REALITY THAT HIS BRAIN TUMOR WAS INOPERABLE; HE STARTED EXAMINING HIS OPTIONS, WHAT HE CALLED HIS PLAN B. AND THIS EXTRAORDINARY PIECE OF MODERN TECHNOLOGY CALLED THE CYBERKNIFE CAME TO HIS ATTENTION.

Developed at Stanford university in the late 80s, the cyberknife is the first and only robotic radio surgery system. Using sophisticated 6D imaging it can treat tumors located anywhere in the body. It delivers radiation beams with pin point accuracy, preventing healthy tissue damage that can occur during traditional radiation treatment.

As this technology is not yet available in South Africa, Clive flew to India three months ago to have Cyberknife treatment. He returned to South Africa feeling much better, confident that the procedure had worked.. The flight back to Bangalore proved grueling but despite his discomfort Clive inevitably began talking cricket

Clive has fond memories of India for it was here, in 1991, that he as captain, led out the SA cricket team to play against India in its first match after SA had been readmitted to international cricket.

Bangalore: population ten million. It’s said that no other city in the world has the power to attract and motivate a casual visitor to move there permanently like Bangalore does. The city is the playground of lndia and attracts vast numbers of hi-tech companies and so has become known as the silicone capital of the world.
In the middle of town one finds the Health Care Global hospitals, which offer a holistic approach to cancer and highly specialized treatment , especially for advanced cancers. All around the hospital are examples of patients who have been successfully treated including this South African, Larry Katz who was treated for stage 4 cancer, and is doing well.
The ever-expanding network of Health care global hospitals in India and Asia are the brainchild of Dr. Ajai Kumar. After working as an oncologist in the United States for 20 years he came back to India and set up the Bangalore Institute of Oncology.
DR KUMAR - So in year 2000 I took a decision, convinced my family, that I had to close my shop there and move to India because that is where I am needed and that is where the challenge is.
After managing to secure a ten million dollar loan he and his team developed a business model, assembled a dedicated group of medical staff and began to give hope.
DR KUMAR - So our goal is we are not satisfied by traditional way of treatment for example when you look at cancer you say palliative care, terminal care. We don’t say that for diabetes, we don’t cure diabetes; you know if a diabetic patient walks I don’t say I’m going to give him palliative care. You know we don’t say that.
Hope is exactly what the hospital had given Clive who, after only four hours sleep, met with Dr. Sridhar who had treated him three months ago.
SOUND UP
Clive discussed his anxiety over his restricted movement but was reassured
SOUND UP – There is a little bit of swelling which usually occurs after the treatment.
After being given medication, the relieved couple spent a quite evening, awaiting the all-important tests the next day. They had to be at the hospital first thing in the morning.
JOHN – It must have been an incredibly difficult drive to the hospital?
SUE RICE – I think it was very quiet, apart for the cow. The holy cow we saw.
His first test was a MRI scan which produces a detailed image of the brain and surrounding nerve tissues.
Then it was time for the important PET scan, which would tell if his cancer was active or had spread to other parts of his body. Here Clive is injected with glucose, which has been tagged with radioactive isotope and which lights up on the pet scan if the glucose is metabolized by any cancer cells
It’s a vital scan because it can tell if treatment is working or not. The hospital provides sophisticated treatment to some Indians and foreigners who can’t afford it.
DR KUMAR - Several people from East African countries we have treated literally free because am a believer that whether Indian or African doesn’t matter, human beings are human beings, cancer is cancer.

It was an anxious wait while his tests were studied.
LINK – WELL CLIVE AND SUE ARE NOW WITH DR. SHRIEDE BECAUSE THE RESULTS FROM THE SCANS ARE NOW AVAILABLE. THE TWO HAVE ASKED FOR SOME PRIVACY WHILE THEY GO THROUGH THOSE RESULTS. WE’LL TAKE A STEP BACK AND THEN HAVE A LOOK AT WHAT THOSE RESULTS ARE.
We arrived to find Dr. Shriede's office crowded with his medical team. They had great news. The cyberknife had done its job.
SOUND UP – Sue: Amazing stuff guys! Dr. Shriede: I think if everything goes well, you can go back on Saturday.
The moment proved too much for Clive who was overcome with emotion. The relief was palpable.
This image depicts the tumor as it was three months ago. There was now no trace of it.
SOUND UP – That is a fantastic response.
The thankful and overjoyed couple shared the news with the family back at home.
SOUND UP - Clive: It’s the doctors here that have sorted it out.
And they are sorting it out for many other South African’s, 15 of whom have travelled to India. While we were there a fellow countryman was having cyberknife therapy for advanced lung cancer. It’s a quick, non-evasive and painless procedure. The treatment costs about 10 thousand dollars, which is a fraction of the cost elsewhere in the world.
Doctors there say that it’s especially effective against prostate cancer. When Greg Fuchsloch was diagnosed , he was advised by two oncologists in Cape Town to have his prostate completely removed, or to have Brachytherapy. He rejected both options after a relative told him about cyberknife.
KARIN: None of the doctors that we saw here actually recommended or even given to us as an option until we…
GREG: As a matter of fact the doctors here had no idea of Cyberknife.
Greg immediately flew to India with his wife. Initially he was a little taken aback at the simplicity of the administration building.
GREG –. But then when you get into the treatment room and you see what that is all about you understand that it is on par with anywhere in the world.
Short bouts of treatments take place over several days leaving lots of time for patients to explore the city in between sessions.
After his treatment greg’s psa levels dropped and he returned to the hpsital in September last year for a final check up.t
JOHN – Wow. ­
SUE - It is wow.
LINK – SPEAK TO THE DOCTORS AT HCG AND THEY WILL TELL YOU THAT CYBERKNIFE ISN’T A CURE FOR CANCER; RATHER IT IS A WAY OF MANAGING THE DISEASE. BUT MORE THAN THAT, IT IS A WAY FOR PEOPLE DESPERATE FOR SOME HOPE TO CLING TO EVEN OUT THE ODDS IN A FIGHT THAT, UP UNTIL NOW, HAS BEEN PRETTY ONE SIDED.
We left India humbled by this group of dedicated doctors whose passion and care for their patients is obvious.
DR KUMAR – To see somebody like Clive Rice, smile and then shake hands and say “you know doc I’m doing good.” That’s it. You don’t want any more. You don’t need any other accolades.
Looking much better, Clive and Sue returned to Johannesburg on the 18th of June.
Movement has retuned to the left side of his body and he could now click his fingers - something he couldn’t do a week before. Cancer survivors often find their lives changing in different directions.
Greg sold his business and is looking at new green ventures.
GREG – It has an impact in the way that we think about things and the way that we conduct our everyday lives.
His wife Karin has started an Ozone therapy center and the couple is planning to move to the country.
Clive is determined to encourage local companies to bring cyberknife to South Africa to help others.
CLIVE – And if there is an opportunity to do it, I definitely want to see if we can make that facility available.

In the meantime he can’t wait to get back to the golf course or race his beloved racing car.
